Social Services Alternative
The social services alternative consists of a variety of programs on a citywide basis directed primarily toward improving the quality of community services and developing viable urban communities. All the block grant funds would be utilized to fund programs such as the Housing Service Center, Filipino Service Center, Black Council on Alcoholism, Alviso Library, Mayfair Community Garden, Mayfair Family Health Center, and other social services that qualify as eligible activities under the Community Development Block Grant guidelines. In order to have eligible Social Services programs, they would have to be centered upon designated CNRAs. Therefore, some physical improvement programs would also be included in the alternative.
Positive environmental impacts will be felt by the human environment and will be measured chiefly in terms of an improvement in the quality and quantity of community services.
The social services alternative plan contains few of the environmental impacts related to the proposed plan and contains no significant negative environmental impacts of any kind. The relative merit, then, of the proposed plan in comparison with the alternative plan lies in the value that is inherent in its specific projects, despite its limited effect upon reducing or eliminating the physical aspects of residential blight.
C. NO PROJECT ALTERNATIVE
A "no project" alternative would forego attempts to achieve the objectives of the Housing and Community Development Act and the objectives of the proposed plan. The attempt to eliminate slums and blighting influences, the elimination of conditions detrimental to health, safety and public welfare through code enforcement, demolition and rehabilitation assistance, the expansion and the improvement of community services for persons of low and moderate income, the improvement of local streets, the attempt to improve public facilities for the handicapped, and the other goals and objectives described in the Project Description would be precluded if no plan were developed.
The "no project" alternative then would presume that all the beneficial impacts of the proposed plan and the other suggested alternatives would not be attained. The prospects for the future quality of housing and neighborhood appearance if the plan is not adopted is uncertain, but the near term trend appears to be one of further deterioration. In addition to a lack of funds from the private sector, failure to utilize the federal monies available through the Housing and Community Development Act will make neighborhood improvement dependent upon uncertain and historically insufficient local public revenues. The city's various partially completed redevelopment projects would represent a serious financial obligation to the city if it were unable to receive CDBG funds.
